The World Health Organization characterises COVID-19 as a pandemic; public-health measures, travel restrictions, healthcare pressures and economic disruption affect almost every region.
COVID-19 vaccines are developed, tested, authorised and deployed at unprecedented speed; access, safety communication, inequity and long-term effects become major public debates.
Global protests against racial injustice grow after the killing of George Floyd in the United States; movements reflect longer histories of policing, discrimination and colonial legacies.
The United Kingdom leaves the European Union’s single market and customs union at the end of the transition period, following Brexit.
Taliban forces return to power in Afghanistan after the withdrawal of US and allied forces; humanitarian and rights conditions, especially for women and girls, become major international concerns.
COP26 in Glasgow produces the Glasgow Climate Pact and renewed commitments, while countries continue to debate the pace and fairness of climate action.
Russia launches a full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February; the war drives displacement, sanctions, military support, energy shifts and renewed European security debate.
The global food and energy markets face severe disruption amid the war in Ukraine, sanctions, supply problems and climate-related shocks.
Generative AI systems become widely accessible to the public, triggering new debates about productivity, education, authorship, misinformation, labour and safety.
The World Health Organization ends the COVID-19 Public Health Emergency of International Concern designation; this does not mean the virus has disappeared or all impacts have ended.
The United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals reach the midpoint of their 2030 agenda; reports highlight uneven progress across countries and goals.

Hamas-led attacks in Israel and the subsequent Israeli military campaign in Gaza produce a major war and humanitarian catastrophe, with regional escalation and extensive international legal and diplomatic debate.
COP28 in Dubai concludes with a global stocktake and an agreement to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems, alongside disputes about implementation and finance.
The Israel–Gaza war and regional escalation drive urgent diplomatic, humanitarian and legal debates; reported casualty figures and legal proceedings require dated updates.
Generative AI and advanced machine-learning systems expand rapidly in public services, research, business and education; governance, copyright, compute, labour and safety debates intensify.
COP29 in Baku produces a new climate-finance goal for developing countries, while disagreements continue over adequacy, responsibility and delivery.
The European Union adopts the AI Act, a major risk-based legal framework for artificial intelligence; phased implementation follows.
The 2024 Summer Olympic Games take place in Paris; global sport remains a cultural arena shaped by diplomacy, inequality and national identity.
Donald Trump begins a second term as president of the United States; changes in trade, climate, migration and foreign policy become major international developments.
The United Nations marks its 80th anniversary, reflecting on collective security, peacekeeping, human rights, development and the limitations of multilateral institutions.
COP30 takes place in Belém, Brazil, from 10–22 November; its outcome package includes climate-finance and adaptation decisions, while implementation and adequacy remain contested.
The International Year of Quantum Science and Technology is observed under the UN system, highlighting a century of quantum physics and its modern applications.
Major geopolitical tensions continue across Europe, the Middle East and parts of Asia; individual ceasefires and negotiations should be dated and re-checked because outcomes remain fluid.

The United States announces a large-scale military strike in Venezuela and reports the capture and removal of Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores; legal, diplomatic and regional consequences continue to be contested and developing.
The 81st session of the UN General Assembly opens in September, continuing diplomacy on conflict, development, rights, climate and multilateral reform.

The Russia–Ukraine war remains unresolved and continues to shape European security, diplomacy, sanctions and military planning; current reporting as of 27 October 2026 describes continued fighting and talks without a comprehensive ceasefire.

The UN recognises International Years for the Woman Farmer, Volunteers for Sustainable Development, and Rangelands and Pastoralists, reflecting international attention to food systems, civic participation and land management.
Ancient Southwest Asia and the Nile

— Major rulers / reference names: Enmebaragesi (historical status and dating debated), Sargon of Akkad, Naram-Sin, Ur-Nammu, Shulgi, Hammurabi, Tiglath-Pileser III, Sargon II, Sennacherib, Ashurbanipal, Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II. Political forms ranged from city-state to territorial empire; king lists and reign lengths are not all equally secure.

— Key rulers: Narmer/Menes (traditional unifier), Djoser, Sneferu, Khufu, Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Amenhotep III, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun, Seti I, Ramesses II and Ramesses III. Many additional pharaohs are preserved in king lists; co-regencies and dynastic dates can differ between reference works.

— Prominent reference names include Suppiluliuma I and Hattusili III (Hittite), Ahiram as a Phoenician epigraphic reference, and kings such as David, Solomon, Omri, Hezekiah and Josiah in biblical / Levantine history. Each ruler’s evidence base differs; biblical tradition should be read alongside archaeology and inscriptions.

— Cyrus II, Cambyses II, Darius I, Xerxes I, Artaxerxes I, Darius II, Artaxerxes II, Artaxerxes III and Darius III. Major themes: satrapies, royal roads, tribute, imperial multilingualism, court ceremonial and conflicts with Greek states.

— Parthian rulers include Mithridates I, Mithridates II and later Vologases kings; Sasanian rulers include Ardashir I, Shapur I, Shapur II, Kavad I, Khosrow I and Khosrow II. Reign numbering varies between dynastic sources.

— Prominent figures: Solon and Cleisthenes (Athens), Leonidas (Sparta), Pericles, Philip II, Alexander the Great, Ptolemy I, Seleucus I and Antiochus III. Greek history is a patchwork of poleis, leagues, kingdoms and empires rather than one continuous monarchy.

— Traditional kings include Romulus, Numa Pompilius and the Tarquins; Republican names include Cincinnatus, the Gracchi, Marius, Sulla, Pompey, Julius Caesar, Cicero and Cato. Imperial reference sequence: Augustus; Julio-Claudians (Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius, Nero); Flavians (Vespasian, Titus, Domitian); adoptive emperors (Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius); Severans (Septimius Severus, Caracalla); Diocletian, Constantine, Theodosius I; western emperors through Romulus Augustulus (476) and continuing eastern Byzantine emperors.

— Major rulers: Constantine I, Theodosius I, Justinian I, Heraclius, Basil II, Alexios I Komnenos, John III Vatatzes, Michael VIII Palaiologos and Constantine XI. The state called Byzantine by modern historians considered itself Roman; the empire ended in 1453.

— Maurya: Chandragupta Maurya, Bindusara, Ashoka. Kushan: Kujula Kadphises, Vima Kadphises, Kanishka (chronology disputed). Gupta: Chandragupta I, Samudragupta, Chandragupta II, Kumaragupta I, Skandagupta. Chola: Vijayalaya, Rajaraja I, Rajendra I and later rulers. The subcontinent contained many contemporaneous regional powers not represented by these names.

— Xia (traditional; historicity debated), Shang, Zhou, Qin, Han, Three Kingdoms, Jin, Northern/Southern dynasties, Sui, Tang, Five Dynasties/Ten Kingdoms, Song, Yuan, Ming, Qing. Prominent rulers: Wu Ding, King Wen and King Wu of Zhou (traditional accounts), Qin Shi Huang, Han Gaozu, Han Wudi, Guangwu, Taizong of Tang, Wu Zetian, Xuanzong, Taizu of Song, Kublai Khan, Hongwu, Yongle, Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong.

— Yamato court; Nara and Heian eras; Kamakura shogunate; Ashikaga / Muromachi shogunate; Sengoku period; Tokugawa shogunate. Prominent leaders and rulers: Prince Shōtoku (traditional attribution), Empress Suiko, Emperor Kanmu, Minamoto no Yoritomo, Ashikaga Takauji, Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, Tokugawa Ieyasu and Tokugawa Yoshimune.

— Genghis Khan, Ögedei, Güyük, Möngke and Kublai; later regional lines include Golden Horde, Chagatai Khanate, Ilkhanate and Yuan. Timur founded a separate conquest empire in Central Asia; he was not a direct Mongol khan.

— Pyu and early mainland states; Pagan/Bagan; Khmer / Angkor (Jayavarman II, Suryavarman II, Jayavarman VII); Champa; Srivijaya; Majapahit (Hayam Wuruk and Gajah Mada are prominent); Ayutthaya; Đại Việt / Vietnam; later Toungoo, Konbaung and Nguyễn dynasties.
Islamic polities, Africa and the Americas

— Rashidun caliphs: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali. Umayyads: Muawiya I, Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I. Abbasids: al-Mansur, Harun al-Rashid, al-Ma’mun. Other important states: Fatimids, Ayyubids (Saladin), Mamluks, Seljuks, Almoravids, Almohads, Umayyads of Córdoba and later regional sultanates. Political and religious authority took multiple forms.

— Early rulers include Osman I (traditional founder), Orhan and Murad I; major sultans include Mehmed II, Selim I, Suleiman I, Ahmed I, Mahmud II and Abdülhamid II. The sultanate is abolished in 1922; the caliphate is abolished in 1924.

— Ghana/Wagadou, Mali, Songhai, Kanem-Bornu, Hausa city-states, Benin, Oyo, Kongo, Asante and Great Zimbabwe. Prominent names include Sunjata Keita, Mansa Musa, Sunni Ali, Askia Muhammad, Ewuare and Osei Tutu; many societies used oral traditions alongside archaeology and external written records.

— Aksumite rulers include Ezana; later Ethiopian dynasties include Zagwe and Solomonic lines. Swahili city-states such as Kilwa, Mombasa and Zanzibar were linked to inland African economies and Indian Ocean routes.

— Olmec centres predate Maya city-states; Classic and Postclassic Maya rulers are often known from inscriptions and city-specific dynastic lists. Mexica / Aztec rulers include Itzcoatl, Moctezuma I, Axayacatl, Ahuitzotl and Moctezuma II; Tlacaelel was an influential political adviser, not a tlatoani.

— Norte Chico / Caral, Chavín, Moche, Nazca, Tiwanaku, Wari, Chimú and Inca traditions developed in different periods. Prominent Inca rulers in later dynastic traditions include Pachacuti, Topa Inca Yupanqui, Huayna Capac, Huáscar and Atahualpa; Spanish conquest and internal conflict shaped the empire’s fall.

— Mississippian centres including Cahokia, Pueblo societies, Haudenosaunee / Iroquois confederacy, Inuit histories, Pacific Northwest communities and many other Indigenous nations. These histories cannot be reduced to a single dynasty list; political forms include cities, confederacies, chiefdoms and mobile societies.
Europe, Russia and the Atlantic world

— Carolingian rulers: Charlemagne and successors; Capetian and Valois kings in France; Plantagenet and Tudor/Stuart monarchs in England; Habsburg rulers in central Europe; Spanish Habsburgs; Bourbon France; Portuguese Avis and Braganza dynasties. Succession branches and contested claims require separate study.

— Kievan Rus’ princes; Muscovy rulers including Ivan III and Ivan IV; Romanov rulers including Peter I, Catherine II, Alexander II, Nicholas II. The Soviet period is not a dynasty and has a distinct party-state leadership chronology.

— Presidents and political leaders should be studied with constitutional chronology, not treated as kings. Founding-era leaders include George Washington, Thomas Jefferson and James Madison; Abraham Lincoln during the Civil War; Franklin D. Roosevelt during the Great Depression and Second World War; later presidents are included where their policies or crises are historically significant.

— Independence and nation-building leaders include Toussaint Louverture, Jean-Jacques Dessalines, Simón Bolívar, José de San Martín, Miguel Hidalgo, José María Morelos and Bernardo O’Higgins. Later political histories are republic-based and cannot be usefully represented as dynastic succession.
China — Ming and Qing succession guides

— Compact sequence: Hongwu (1368–1398); Jianwen (1398–1402); Yongle (1402–1424); Hongxi (1424–1425); Xuande (1425–1435); Zhengtong (1435–1449); Jingtai (1449–1457); Tianshun (1457–1464); Chenghua (1464–1487); Hongzhi (1487–1505); Zhengde (1505–1521); Jiajing (1521–1567); Longqing (1567–1572); Wanli (1572–1620); Taichang (1620); Tianqi (1620–1627); Chongzhen (1627–1644). Reign transitions, regencies and court power require separate study.

— Compact sequence: Nurhaci (founding leader); Hong Taiji; Shunzhi; Kangxi; Yongzheng; Qianlong; Jiaqing; Daoguang; Xianfeng; Tongzhi; Guangxu; Xuantong / Puyi. Qing authority expands across a multiethnic empire; nineteenth-century military, fiscal and diplomatic crises culminate in the 1911 Revolution and the end of imperial rule in 1912.

— Norman: William I, William II, Henry I, Stephen (with a disputed civil-war succession), Henry II. Plantagenet and branches: Richard I, John, Henry III, Edward I, Edward II, Edward III, Richard II; Lancastrians Henry IV, Henry V, Henry VI; Yorkists Edward IV, Edward V, Richard III. Tudor: Henry VII, Henry VIII, Edward VI, Mary I, Elizabeth I. Stuart: James I, Charles I, Charles II, James II, William III and Mary II, Anne. Hanover: George I, George II, George III, George IV, William IV, Victoria. Modern: Edward VII, George V, Edward VIII, George VI, Elizabeth II, Charles III. The political system changes radically over these centuries; dates and claims should be checked for contested transitions.

— Capetian kings and branches precede Valois rulers; major names include Philip II, Louis IX, Philip IV, Charles V, Charles VII and Louis XI. Bourbon monarchs include Henry IV, Louis XIII, Louis XIV, Louis XV and Louis XVI. Revolution abolishes the monarchy in 1792; Napoleon I becomes emperor in 1804. Later regimes include Bourbon Restoration, July Monarchy, Second Republic, Second Empire under Napoleon III, and the republics. Modern France is a republic, not a continuation of royal succession.

— Kievan Rus’ and regional principalities; Muscovy under Ivan III and Ivan IV; Romanov sequence includes Michael I, Alexis, Peter I, Anna, Elizabeth, Catherine II, Paul I, Alexander I, Nicholas I, Alexander II, Alexander III and Nicholas II. The monarchy ends in 1917; the Soviet Union is led by party-state leaders rather than a hereditary royal dynasty.

— Portugal’s Avis and Braganza dynasties, and Spain’s Trastámara, Habsburg and Bourbon lines, are central to early oceanic expansion. Key rulers include João II and Manuel I of Portugal; Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon; Charles I / Emperor Charles V; Philip II, Philip III, Philip IV and later Bourbon rulers. Spain’s political union and imperial structures changed over time; Portugal and Spain should not be treated as one continuous state.

— Court lineages are traditionally traced through the imperial house, but early dates are often legendary or reconstructed. Shogunal sequence: Kamakura — Minamoto no Yoritomo and later Hōjō regents; Ashikaga / Muromachi — Ashikaga Takauji and successors; Sengoku era — rival daimyō including Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu; Tokugawa shogunate (1603–1868) from Ieyasu through the later Tokugawa shoguns, ending with Tokugawa Yoshinobu. Shoguns, emperors, regents and regional daimyō held different kinds of power.

Teaching Architecture, Curriculum Sequencing, Assessment and Project Ladder
School computer classes often emphasize device operation, keyboarding and office applications.
Block programming and introductory computing spread in schools.

CBSE’s CT & AI curriculum context includes Classes III-VIII. Verify the live official curriculum for updates before planning a specific year’s lesson. 34.1 Age-flexible learning bands L0 - Classes III-V: concrete exploration Computer parts; safe use; mouse/keyboard; files; drawing; typing; patterns; sequencing; unplugged algorithms; block-based stories. Digital citizenship; trusted adult/reporting; simple data tables; charts; visual presentations; basic AI awareness and verification. Assessment: perform a task, explain steps, create a small artifact, identify safe/unsafe choices. L1 - Classes VI-VIII: connected concepts File organization; productivity tools; search literacy; spreadsheets; data charts; variables; conditions; loops; events. Internet/network ideas; privacy; cybersecurity habits; simple website; block/text bridge; sensors or microcontroller preview. Assessment: small portfolio; debug a project; cite sources; interpret a chart; explain network and privacy choices. L2 - Classes IX-X: formal foundations Text programming; functions; collections; files; web foundations; number representation; logic; algorithms; SQL introduction. Data collection; statistics; cybersecurity; computational thinking; AI/data literacy; integrated project. Assessment: code plus tests; written explanation; data report; design artifact; short demonstration. L3 - Classes XI-XII: systematic subject study Programming; data structures; algorithms; databases; computer systems; networks; AI/IT board-specific content and project. Assessment: examinations plus practicals; project documentation; oral defence; evidence of testing and attribution. L4 - UG foundation Discrete maths; programming; data structures/algorithms; architecture; OS; networks; databases; software engineering; theory. Assessment: implementation, proofs, system labs, team engineering and written technical communication. L5 - Advanced UG / specialization Electives; substantial team project; advanced systems/data/AI/security; research reading; open-ended design. Assessment: baseline comparison, architecture decisions, security review, performance measurements and maintainability. L6 - MTech / research Specialist depth; research literature; rigorous experiment; formal/empirical methods; thesis/capstone; critical review. Assessment: reproducible artifact; research report; defence; external evaluation; limitations and future work. 34.2 Teaching sequence templates Concept lesson: familiar example -> vocabulary -> diagram/model -> worked example -> guided practice -> independent task -> review. Programming lesson: goal -> trace/algorithm -> predict -> implement -> test -> debug -> improve -> explain. Data lesson: question -> data provenance -> clean/inspect -> summarize -> visualize -> interpret uncertainty -> communicate. Systems lesson: need -> components -> interface -> data/control flow -> failure case -> test -> trade-off. AI lesson: task -> non-AI baseline -> data/model idea -> demonstration -> evaluation -> limitations/risks -> human review. Project lesson: problem -> stakeholders -> scope -> plan -> prototype -> test -> review -> document -> present -> archive. 34.3 Project ladder across ages L0: digital self-portrait; safe-search poster; pattern-based animation; step-by-step recipe algorithm; small class survey and bar chart. L1: interactive story; keyboard skills dashboard; spreadsheet budget; accessible poster; website with source credits; sensor reading. L2: text adventure; calculator; CSV analysis; personal portfolio; simple database; network diagram; password-safety explainer. L3: CRUD application; SQL reporting; data visualizer; small game; API client; algorithm benchmarking; simple ML evaluation. L4: command-line tool; file indexer; web service with tests; database-backed app; OS/network lab; secure coding exercise. L5: distributed service; compiler/interpreter; ML pipeline; accessibility audit; threat model and penetration test in an authorized lab. L6: reproduce a paper; design a new algorithm; evaluate a model; prototype a specialized system; benchmark hardware; conduct a controlled user study. 34.4 Universal lesson-planning fields Learner age band; prerequisites; learning objectives; vocabulary; concept dependencies; misconceptions. Demonstration; learner activity; inclusive adaptations; safety note; material/software; time budget. Formative check; rubric; product/evidence; reflection; extension; remediation; source list; revision date. Separate intended learning outcome from tool brand; avoid assuming access to a paid device, fast Internet or English-only materials. 34.5 Assessment design Recall: define, label, identify, list. Understanding: compare, classify, explain, draw a model. Application: run, configure, implement, calculate, use a tool safely. Analysis: debug, trace, inspect data, decompose, find a bottleneck. Evaluation: justify trade-offs, assess evidence, review safety and accessibility. Creation: design, build, test, document, present and maintain. Evidence: code, diagrams, notebooks, test logs, reflection, presentation, project artefact and oral defence.

B. Self-learning route by goal Teach school computer education: 01 -> 03 -> 08 (block and text programming) -> 16 (data) -> 18 (web) -> 19 (safety) -> 34 (lesson architecture). Use 34’s age band and project ladder.

Become a robotics/embedded engineer: 04 -> 05 -> 07 -> 08 -> 25 -> 06/12/17 -> 20/21/22 as needed -> safety and real-time validation.

E. Universal checklist before teaching any topic What real-world problem does the topic address?
What prior concept does it depend on? What can be safely skipped at the learner’s entry level?
What is the smallest useful mental model, diagram or analogy?
What vocabulary must the student be able to recognize and use?
What should be seen, predicted, built, tested, debugged or explained?
What are the common misconceptions and boundary cases?
What data, device, account or third-party service is required? Is there an offline alternative?
What are the safety, privacy, security, accessibility and copyright considerations?
What evidence demonstrates learning, rather than just tool familiarity?
What is the natural next topic, and how will the idea reappear at greater depth?
